project_and_compatibility.implementation_language: Testplane is implemented primarily in TypeScript and runs on Node.js. Tests are authored in TypeScript or JavaScript with Mocha syntax, async functions, WebdriverIO-style browser commands, and expect-webdriverio assertions. Go is not required for the test suite. [S1][S2][S5]
project_and_compatibility.node_and_typescript_compatibility: [uncertain] Testplane 9.1.1 declares Node.js >=22, its CI was moved to Node 24 in July 2026, and the npm artifact was published with Node 24.19.0, so Node 24 and npm are directly supported. It transpiles TypeScript through bundled esbuild or optional SWC and requires separate `tsc` type checking. The package itself is built with TypeScript 5.3.2 and ts-node 10.9.1; no official source certifies TypeScript 6 or the repository's exact module configuration, and no project installation was executed. ESM and explicit imports are supported on Node 22+, but TypeScript 6 remains an empirical gate. [S1][S2][S5][S7]
project_and_compatibility.operating_system_support: [uncertain] The framework supports local and remote execution on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Official local-browser documentation lists Chrome and Firefox support on Ubuntu 20.04, 22.04, and 24.04, and the project updated Ubuntu 24.04 dependencies on 2026-08-21. GitHub-hosted Ubuntu is officially documented. Native Safari requires macOS or a remote grid. The npm package is portable JavaScript, but an authoritative Linux arm64 matrix for downloaded browsers, drivers, and system packages was not found. [S3][S6][S15]
project_and_compatibility.license_and_governance: Testplane core is MIT licensed. Package metadata states that the source is published and distributed by Yandex LLC as owner, while development occurs publicly under the gemini-testing organization and seven npm maintainers are listed. Governance is maintainer/company-led: no foundation charter, elected steering model, public succession plan, or repository security policy was found. The MIT license imposes no material repository-use restriction beyond preserving its notice. [S1][S2][S16]
project_and_compatibility.installation_model: Install with `npm install -D testplane@9` or scaffold with `npm init testplane@latest`. The wizard can also install `@testplane/testing-library` and `html-reporter`. `npx testplane install-deps` downloads configured Chrome and Firefox versions, their drivers, and supported Ubuntu packages into `~/.testplane` or `TESTPLANE_BROWSERS_PATH`; missing dependencies can also be downloaded on first run. Edge and Safari browsers are not auto-downloaded. Selenoid/browser images or commercial grids are optional. [S5][S6][S15]
project_and_compatibility.candidate_scope_and_layer: Complete Node.js E2E framework: integrated Mocha-based runner, WebDriver client, assertions, browser management, retries, worker parallelism, browser sets, screenshots and visual comparison, failure history, hooks, plugins, and an interactive report. Sharding and several lifecycle features are official companion plugins rather than core. [S2][S8][S13][S14]
project_and_compatibility.authoring_and_async_model: Native JavaScript and TypeScript async/await with Mocha-style `describe` and `it`, a WebdriverIO-derived browser and element API, polling `expect` matchers, and optional Testing Library queries. Testplane 9 favors explicit imports but `@testplane/globals` can restore global typings. There is no Cypress-style command queue; every asynchronous browser command must be awaited. [S5][S7][S9]
project_and_compatibility.build_pipeline_coupling: Node-environment black-box E2E tests navigate to `baseUrl` and can exercise the existing Parcel build served by Gin or the Parcel development proxy without transforming application source. Testplane's separate browser/component-test mode uses bundled Vite, but that mode is not required for E2E. Visual checks, CDP helpers, and Time Travel inject test-session behavior into the page without replacing the production build pipeline. [S5][S8][S14][S18]
project_and_compatibility.testability_instrumentation_required: Ordinary WebDriver E2E execution requires no production source transform, special route, injected shipped runtime, or relaxed browser security policy. Existing accessible names, visible text, IDs, and CSS selectors are usable; stable `data-testid` attributes are optional where semantic locators are unavailable. A health route is useful for readiness, and deterministic database reset plus server-side Yahoo Finance replacement require test-only harness seams outside Testplane. Time Travel and CDP tooling inject scripts only into controlled sessions. [S9][S11][S12][S18]

browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_engines: Through W3C WebDriver, Testplane can drive installed or remote Chrome/Chromium and Edge, Firefox, and native Safari, plus Appium targets and older browsers supported by their drivers. Local auto-download covers Chrome and Firefox; Edge's driver but not browser can be downloaded, and Safari requires macOS. Ubuntu has no local native Safari/WebKit equivalent. Browser-specific CDP features work only on Chromium. [S6][S7][S8]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_protocol: Testplane 9 uses W3C WebDriver as its only primary automation protocol. WebDriver BiDi/WebSocket support is enabled for compatible Chrome, Edge, and Firefox sessions; Safari did not have documented BiDi support. Chromium CDP remains available through `getPuppeteer` or experimental CDP APIs for network mocks, accessibility snapshots, and emulation, but the former all-CDP `devtools` automation mode was removed because of hard-to-reproduce failures. [S7][S8][S11][S17]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.headless_and_headed_modes: Chrome/Chromium, Firefox, and Edge can run headed for local debugging and headless for CI through configuration. The official GitHub guide requires headless browser execution on hosted Ubuntu and documents Chrome sandbox flags. Remote grids can expose VNC, video, and logs. Native Safari execution is macOS or cloud based rather than an Ubuntu headless path. [S6][S15]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_version_management: `install-deps` can download exact configured Chrome and Firefox versions plus compatible Chrome, Firefox, and Edge drivers, with the cache rooted at `~/.testplane` or `TESTPLANE_BROWSERS_PATH`. Browser versions are set through WebDriver capabilities. Edge and Safari binaries must be supplied by the host or grid. Official documentation warns that ready-made Selenoid images may not contain current browsers; deterministic CI should pin browser versions, cache keys, and container digests. [S6][S15]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.parallel_browser_support: Browser IDs and sets define selected browser combinations. `sessionsPerBrowser`, worker count, process `parallelLimit`, and per-session reuse control local concurrency. The official `@testplane/chunks` plugin deterministically partitions tests across CI jobs, and html-reporter can merge shard reports. There is no single Playwright-style projects object, but the set/browser/plugin model covers matrices and sharding. [S8][S13]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.mobile_emulation: WebDriver capabilities can configure Chromium mobile emulation, viewport, device scale, user agent, touch, and orientation; documented examples use an iPhone 12 Pro profile. Appium/Selenium grids and commercial clouds can supply Android, iOS simulators, or physical devices, and Testplane 9 added iOS 26 screenshot handling. Desktop emulation is not a physical mobile device, and many emulation controls are Chromium/CDP-specific. [S6][S7]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.real_browser_fidelity: WebDriver controls installed vendor browsers, so Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari sessions are real browser products rather than a JavaScript DOM simulation. Native Safari means SafariDriver on macOS or a real cloud device; Chromium emulation and an unrelated WebKit build do not establish Safari behavior. Selenoid/cloud fidelity depends on the selected image, OS, version, and provider, while CDP-only helpers reduce feature parity outside Chromium. [S6][S7]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.environment_determinism_controls: Core configuration controls browser/version, window size, orientation, headless mode, browser capabilities, context isolation, cursor reset, screenshot delay, animation disabling during `assertView`, and network throttling. Puppeteer/CDP can additionally control CPU and Chromium features. There is no unified cross-browser fixture API for clock, timezone, locale, permissions, geolocation, random seeds, all animations, fonts, or reduced motion. Those require capabilities, preload/execute helpers, fixed images/fonts, and repository fixtures. [S8][S10]

application_fit.dynamic_dom_synchronization: [uncertain] Element queries wait for existence, explicit `waitForDisplayed`/`waitForClickable` and general `waitUntil` are available, and expect-webdriverio matchers poll. This should fit HTMX requests, DOM swaps, lazy partials, and Handlebars rendering when each action is followed by a stable visible-state assertion. A retained WebDriver element can become stale after HTMX replaces its node, so selectors or Testing Library queries should be rerun after swaps. No Open Asset Allocator spike verified the exact sequence. [S8][S9][S18]
application_fit.routing_support: Navigo is framework-agnostic to Testplane. Tests can use `browser.url`, relative `baseUrl`, real links, WebDriver back/forward/refresh commands, URL assertions, and route-specific DOM waits. Direct SPA deep links work if Gin or Parcel supplies the application shell for the route. `openAndWait` can wait for selectors, predicates, and Chromium network idle, but route cleanup and History API correctness must be asserted by application-specific tests. [S8][S9][S18]
application_fit.locator_model: Core WebdriverIO-compatible selectors include CSS, XPath, link/text, accessibility `aria/...`, IDs, and shadow DOM. The official `@testplane/testing-library` adapter adds role, label, text, placeholder, display-value, and test-id queries and is included by the project wizard. `$` returns the first match rather than enforcing strict uniqueness, so cardinality must be asserted where ambiguity matters; re-query after HTMX replacements. [S5][S9]
application_fit.form_interaction: WebDriver element commands cover click, set/add/clear value, keyboard actions, focus-sensitive interactions, selects, files, drag, touch, and JavaScript execution. Tests can press Tab or click elsewhere to trigger blur, inspect focus/value/validity, assert synchronized hidden fields, and manipulate dynamic rows through real browser events. Driver differences and custom widgets still require targeted assertions; direct script assignment should not replace user-level interactions under test. [S9]
application_fit.canvas_and_download_support: Chart.js can be validated semantically through `browser.execute` by inspecting the chart instance, canvas dimensions, labels, datasets, and exported values, with stabilized `assertView` checks as secondary evidence. Testplane has screenshot/PDF and upload commands but no documented first-class download event/save stream. True downloads therefore require browser profile preferences plus a worker-specific filesystem directory and polling, or Chromium Puppeteer/CDP code. Filename, completion, content, and cleanup remain harness work. [S9][S10][S18]
application_fit.network_and_api_access: Node-side tests can use Node 24 `fetch` or repository clients to seed REST fixtures. Core `browser.mock` can observe, respond, redirect, or abort browser requests, but official documentation says it works only with CDP, so it is Chromium-specific despite BiDi support. Puppeteer and raw CDP provide deeper Chromium interception. Browser interception cannot replace Yahoo Finance calls made by the Go backend; use a fake upstream service/configuration seam or seeded data for cross-browser determinism. [S11][S18]
application_fit.same_origin_support: Tests can target the consolidated Gin production server or Parcel's development server/proxy through `baseUrl` with no Testplane-specific CORS changes. WebDriver preserves normal browser origin behavior. Cross-origin test flows remain possible through WebDriver window/navigation APIs, while request mocking and some diagnostics may be Chromium-only. [S8][S18]
application_fit.test_isolation: Chrome 93+ defaults to a fresh isolated browser context for tests while reusing the underlying session; other browsers default to no context isolation. `clearSession`, cookies, local/session storage commands, state save/restore, and session recreation provide explicit cleanup. IndexedDB is not included in saved state, and PostgreSQL remains external. Firefox/Safari safety requires explicit browser-state cleanup or low `testsPerSession`, while all browsers need unique server data or disposable databases. [S8]
application_fit.external_server_model: Supported. Each browser has a configurable `baseUrl` and WebDriver grid URL, so the same test suite can target an independently started Parcel/Gin stack, Docker Compose, a local host process, a remote Selenium grid, or a deployed environment on arbitrary reachable ports. Testplane need not own the application process. [S6][S8]
application_fit.application_lifecycle: Core `devServer` starts one command, streams its logs, can reuse an existing server, supports an async or HTTP readiness probe, and stops its child process with the runner; `beforeAll` and `afterAll` support additional setup/cleanup. A Compose command could wrap the stack, but Testplane does not natively model PostgreSQL, Flyway, Gin, Parcel, health dependencies, volumes, and log collection as separate services. This repository should retain Make/GitHub Actions orchestration and use always-running teardown. [S12][S18]
application_fit.visual_regression_workflow: Visual regression is a core strength. `assertView` captures element, viewport, or full-page/composite images, auto-waits for the target, waits for static resources, disables animation, ignores selected elements/caret/antialiasing, supports pixel and color tolerances, and stores per-browser references. Testplane 9 improves long/scrollable elements, sticky overlays, hover suppression, pseudo-elements, and iOS cropping. Open-source html-reporter offers six diff views, one-click review/update, `--update-refs`, static CI reports, and report merging. Pin OS/browser/fonts/viewport and await Chart.js animation before a limited visual assertion. [S7][S10][S14]
application_fit.accessibility_audit_integration: Testing Library queries and computed role/label commands support accessible authoring. Official accessibility guidance uses Puppeteer's Chromium accessibility-tree snapshot and is explicitly Chrome/CDP-only. Current `axe-core` can be injected or called from a custom Testplane helper and serialized to open-source reports, but Testplane has no first-party axe adapter, cross-browser ARIA snapshot matcher, or integrated audit report. [S9][S17]

reliability.waiting_model: Element lookup waits for existence; WebDriver actions and explicit `waitFor*` commands cover visibility, enabled, and clickable states; `expect` assertions poll; `waitUntil` handles application predicates; and navigation has page-load timeouts. `openAndWait` can combine selector, predicate, network-idle, and failed-resource checks, but network-idle/error features are CDP-only. HTMX tests should wait for a post-swap user-visible condition or known request rather than use `pause`. [S8][S9][S11]
reliability.flake_controls: Core controls include per-browser retry counts, conditional `shouldRetry`, test/page/WebDriver/wait timeouts, session rejection patterns, command history, last-failed reruns, process/session recycling, tags, and selective execution. Official plugins add command retry, progressive retry, retry limits, repeat runs, and deterministic chunks. Visual checks disable animations and wait for static resources. Retries can conceal database side effects, so setup/reset must be idempotent and first-attempt failures retained. [S8][S13][S14][S16]
reliability.isolation_model: Chrome 93+ can create an isolated browser context per test while keeping a session warm. Other browsers reuse the session by default and need `clearSession`, hooks, `testsPerSession: 1`, or `reloadSession` for stronger isolation. Node workers and browser sessions are independently bounded. Stateful PostgreSQL scenarios can run serially, but database schemas, transactions, reset, and retry-safe fixture cleanup are repository responsibilities. [S8][S12][S13]
reliability.resource_usage: [uncertain] Testplane 9.1.1 itself is 3.27 MB unpacked but has a broad dependency graph; downloaded browsers and system packages dominate installation size. Official guidance estimates one Linux desktop browser session at roughly 1.2 CPU cores and recommends workers no higher than CPU count. Time Travel averages about 200 KB per compressed DOM snapshot, while screenshots, diffs, reports, grids, and videos add disk/CPU cost. No repository benchmark measured install size, peak memory, CPU, or wall time. [S1][S13][S14]
reliability.parallelism_controls: `sessionsPerBrowser`, worker count, `parallelLimit`, browser sets, and `testsPerSession` give independent concurrency controls. Database-sensitive runs can use one browser session and one worker or a separate serial set, while unrelated read-only suites use greater concurrency. `@testplane/chunks` distributes future CI work. Safe PostgreSQL parallelism still requires worker/shard-specific databases or data namespaces and cannot be inferred from browser-context isolation. [S8][S13][S18]
reliability.flake_observability: HTML reports retain every retry, failure, error, command history, metadata, screenshot diff, and filtering for retried tests. Time Travel modes can record all runs, retries only, or the last failed run; last-failed JSON and repeat plugins help reproduction. JSON/stat reporters enable local post-processing. There is no core long-term quarantine registry, first-attempt trend database, or historical dashboard, so durable flake rates and ownership need repository-owned ingestion or external tooling. [S8][S14][S16]

diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_artifacts: Core failure artifacts include automatic full-page or viewport screenshots, visual expected/actual/diff images, stack traces, source snippets, command history, test metadata, JSONL output, and optional Time Travel DOM snapshots. html-reporter stores results in SQLite and exposes retries and logs. Selenoid/cloud grids can add video, VNC, driver, network, and console logs. Complete HAR/network archives and video are not uniform core artifacts, and backend/Compose logs remain separate. [S8][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.debugging_tools: `npx testplane gui` provides live execution, screenshots, diffs, command history, targeted reruns, and CI-report inspection. Headed mode, `browser.debug`, Node inspector, REPL before/on failure, `switchToRepl`, keep-browser-on-fail, a VS Code extension, and Time Travel DOM replay cover interactive and postmortem debugging. Time Travel replays DOM state rather than a video and does not yet provide a complete network timeline. [S14][S16]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.test_generation: The project wizard creates configuration and an example test, while Testing Library helpers improve locator authoring. No maintained deterministic core recorder/code generator comparable to Playwright codegen was documented. Optional Testplane AI/CLI and agent tooling can inspect pages and reports, but generated tests still require human review and AI is not necessary for authoring or execution. [S5][S14][S16]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.reporters: Core terminal reporters include flat, plain, and JSONL with file output and multiple-reporter support. Official organization packages provide JSON, statistics, TeamCity, and the feature-rich html-reporter; custom reporters can subscribe to runner events. HTML reports can merge SQLite/data sources across shards. No first-party JUnit reporter was found in the current official catalog, so GitHub test annotations or JUnit XML require a community/custom converter. [S13][S14][S16]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.documentation_quality: The current v9 site is extensive, versioned, searchable, bilingual, and contains guides, command/config references, migration material, examples, a blog, and source edit links. It is actively maintained in 2026. Accuracy is uneven at edges: some current CI examples still use unsupported Node 20 or older action versions, the browser reference displays removed `devtools` values before correcting them, and tolerance defaults conflict within one page. Setup claims should be checked against v9 package metadata and migration notes. [S5][S7][S8][S15]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.local_workflow: Run all tests with `npx testplane`, select a path, test name with `--grep`, tag, set, or browser, use `--last-failed-only`, and update references with `--update-refs`. GUI/headed mode supports visual iteration, REPL and inspector support breakpoints, keep-browser preserves a failed session, and official repeat/last-failed tools aid reproduction. Focused local workflow is strong, although plugin installation and configuration add more moving parts than a single-package runner. [S8][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_log_correlation: Testplane adds a unique X-Request-ID containing per-test/retry and per-WebDriver-request identifiers to grid traffic and records test PID, browser/session metadata, timestamps, command history, and reports. Dev-server logs are prefixed and streamed. Browser application requests do not automatically receive that WebDriver header, and Gin, Flyway, PostgreSQL, and Compose logs are not ingested into one timeline. The CI harness should propagate its own run/test ID and upload UTC-stamped service logs beside reports. [S8][S12][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.artifact_data_exposure: Screenshots, visual baselines/diffs, Time Travel DOM snapshots, SQLite/JSON reports, command arguments, browser/grid logs, state files, videos, and network mock calls can expose portfolio data, credentials, cookies, tokens, or downloaded statements. Official authorization guidance warns not to commit state files, and a 2025 fix removed tokens from unhandled-rejection logs. There is no universal artifact-redaction layer. Use synthetic data, selective logging, restricted artifacts, short retention, secret masking, and disable unnecessary Time Travel/body capture. [S2][S8][S14]

github_actions_fit.official_ci_support: The maintained `gemini-testing/gh-actions-testplane@v1` action runs Testplane, caches local browsers, writes failed-test statistics to the job summary, and returns HTML-report path and exit-code outputs. Official docs target GitHub-hosted Ubuntu and standard checkout/setup-node actions. The action itself uses Node 20 internally, which GitHub Actions supports, but current documentation examples specifying application Node 20 conflict with Testplane 9's Node >=22 requirement and must be changed to Node 24. [S1][S15][S20]
github_actions_fit.browser_caching: The official action automatically caches local browsers, while npm dependencies use setup-node's npm cache. Manual workflows can cache `TESTPLANE_BROWSERS_PATH` keyed by OS, architecture, browser/version, Testplane lockfile, and system image. Browser system packages are runner-image state rather than portable cache content. Pinning explicit versions is safer than reusing an unversioned cache, and Edge/Safari remain externally managed. [S6][S15][S20]
github_actions_fit.artifact_integration: The official action exposes `html-report-path`; documentation shows `actions/upload-artifact@v4` under `if: always()` and optional GitHub Pages publishing. Screenshots, diffs, SQLite, Time Travel snapshots, JSONL, browser/grid logs, and Compose logs can be uploaded as standard artifacts. Privacy, retention, naming, and non-report service-log collection remain workflow configuration. [S14][S15][S20]
github_actions_fit.sharding_and_matrix_support: Use a GitHub matrix with the official `@testplane/chunks` count/run parameters to partition tests, optionally add browser/set axes, upload each HTML report, and run `html-reporter merge-reports` in an aggregation job. Retries occur within a shard; a GitHub job retry reruns the shard. Official examples use S3, but GitHub artifacts can replace it with custom download/merge steps. Database-mutating shards require independent PostgreSQL instances or serial execution. [S13][S15]
github_actions_fit.container_compatibility: Testplane can run on the Ubuntu host beside this repository's Docker Compose stack or connect to Selenoid/Selenium browser containers. Host execution avoids container-to-host browser networking complexity. If browsers are containerized, the application must bind to a reachable interface and use service/host-gateway DNS because container localhost is not the Compose host. Ready-made Selenoid images may lag current browsers, and the project still has an open issue to build current browser images. [S6][S18][S21]
github_actions_fit.failure_cleanup: Testplane normally closes sessions and its `devServer` child and provides `afterAll`, but Compose services, PostgreSQL volumes, Flyway state, downloaded files, and independently started processes need workflow cleanup guarded by `if: always()`. Cancellation can bypass process hooks, so use disposable runners/databases, unique Compose project names, timeouts, idempotent pre-run cleanup, and an always-running `docker compose down --volumes --remove-orphans` step after log collection. [S12][S15][S18]

cost_and_risk.open_source_completeness: Core runner, local Chrome/Firefox management, WebDriver execution, retries, parallelism, visual comparison, screenshots, command history, state tools, and Time Travel are MIT-licensed. Official open-source companions provide Testing Library, HTML/JSON reports, GitHub Action, chunks, repeat/retry plugins, and VS Code integration. No paid service is required for the repository's Ubuntu Chrome/Firefox baseline, but Safari/real devices need owned infrastructure or a provider. [S1][S13][S14][S16]
cost_and_risk.optional_cloud_dependency: BrowserStack, Sauce Labs, and other Selenium/Appium grids are optional for native Safari, physical devices, OS/version breadth, VNC, provider video, and high concurrency. Equivalent basic local Chrome/Firefox execution, visual baselines, reports, retries, sharding, and DOM replay are available without a cloud. Hosted long-term analytics and broad real-device coverage have no complete local equivalent, but they are not required for base CI. [S6][S13][S14]
cost_and_risk.migration_cost: Medium to high. Async JavaScript/TypeScript, CSS/ARIA/Testing Library selectors, Mocha structure, REST fixtures, and WebDriver concepts transfer. Testplane browser helpers, `assertView`, config inheritance, context injection, plugin events, html-reporter SQLite, retries, sets/chunks, and visual baselines are framework-specific. Keeping page/domain fixtures, API clients, and database lifecycle independent from Testplane reduces lock-in. [S5][S8][S10][S13]
cost_and_risk.security_and_supply_chain: [uncertain] Positive evidence includes MIT source, npm integrity signatures, SLSA provenance attestation, a GitHub OIDC trusted publisher, lockfile releases, and active vulnerability work. Risks include many direct/transitive dependencies, browser/driver and Ubuntu-package downloads, plugin code with host privileges, executable browser grids, report custom scripts, and the absence of a visible repository SECURITY.md or published vulnerability-response process. No npm audit, image scan, SBOM, license scan, or provenance-chain review was performed. Pin lockfiles/images, use `npm ci`, restrict CI permissions/egress, and scan downloaded artifacts. [S1][S2][S16][S21]
cost_and_risk.custom_harness_burden: Moderate. Testplane supplies browser management, waits, retries, Chrome isolation, visual regression, dev-server readiness, workers, sharding, reports, and diagnostics. Repository code remains necessary for multi-service Compose/Flyway/Gin readiness, disposable PostgreSQL state, worker-safe test data and downloads, server-side Yahoo Finance replacement, cross-browser state cleanup, axe integration, backend-log correlation, artifact redaction, and guaranteed teardown. [S8][S12][S13][S18]
cost_and_risk.capability_delivery_tier: Core OSS: Mocha runner, WebDriver/BiDi sessions, TypeScript transpilation, local browser management, waits/assertions, retries, Chrome contexts, browser sets/workers, screenshots, `assertView`, state commands, command history, last-failed mode, and Time Travel recording. Official OSS companions: Testing Library locators, html/json/stat reporters, GitHub Action, chunks, global hooks, repeat/retry tools, Storybook, VS Code, and AI/CLI tooling. Chromium/CDP only: request mocking, deep network/CPU emulation, and accessibility snapshots. Custom: Compose/Flyway/PostgreSQL lifecycle, backend Yahoo stub, downloads, axe reporting, non-Chromium isolation cleanup, JUnit conversion, and service-log correlation. Paid/owned infrastructure: optional real devices, native Safari, and large remote grids. [S6][S11][S13][S14][S16][S17]
cost_and_risk.ai_execution_boundary: Normal Testplane authoring, browser execution, retries, visual comparison, reporting, and CI require no LLM, model credential, AI egress, or per-run AI fee. `testplane-ai`, Testplane Skill, MCP, and CLI agent features are optional authoring/debugging aids. Keep them outside required CI, expose only synthetic data and least-privilege credentials, and commit reviewed deterministic tests that retain non-AI GUI, REPL, selector, and report workflows. [S14][S16]

evidence_and_decision.confidence: High confidence for version, package metadata, Node support, maintenance activity, npm counts, browser/config behavior, visual tooling, and CI integration because they come from current official docs and live npm/GitHub APIs. Medium confidence for application fit, isolation behavior outside Chrome, ecosystem production use, and supply-chain judgment because they require project-specific execution or unavailable private adoption data. Low confidence for TypeScript 6 compatibility, architecture support, resource cost, and the weighted score because no project spike or benchmark was run.
evidence_and_decision.hard_gate_result: [uncertain] Provisional pass with mandatory spike outstanding. Pass by documented capability: complete E2E runner; Node 24/npm; TypeScript authoring path; Linux/GitHub Ubuntu; black-box Parcel/Gin execution; Chrome/Firefox plus remote Safari; HTMX/Navigo/form/canvas automation; external baseUrl; open-source visual regression; retries; controlled parallelism; official GitHub Action; sharding/report merge; and Docker compatibility. Conditional pass: TypeScript 6 types were not run; Firefox/Safari need explicit state cleanup; reliable cross-browser Yahoo replacement must be server-side; downloads, axe, Compose/Flyway/PostgreSQL lifecycle, and backend-log correlation need custom harness code. Not verified: the complete application spike, browser matrix, artifact privacy, and resource benchmark. [S1][S5][S6][S8][S10][S13][S15][S18]
evidence_and_decision.deal_breakers: No confirmed exclusion-level incompatibility. It should be excluded if the project requires tested TypeScript 6 compatibility without a separate E2E tsconfig, local Safari/WebKit on Ubuntu, first-class download objects, uniform cross-browser request interception, fresh browser contexts for every Firefox/Safari test, built-in JUnit/axe output, or zero custom Compose/PostgreSQL harness. A project spike exposing stale-element failures, v9 visual instability, Node 24/TS6 type errors, or unsafe database retry behavior would also be a deal breaker.
evidence_and_decision.project_fit_score: [uncertain] Provisional 77.6/100. Category scores: application fit 83/100 x 30% = 24.9; maintenance 87/100 x 20% = 17.4; reliability 82/100 x 15% = 12.3; adoption 46/100 x 15% = 6.9; GitHub Actions experience 81/100 x 10% = 8.1; diagnostics 89/100 x 5% = 4.45; cost and risk 71/100 x 5% = 3.55. Strengths are visual regression, Chrome isolation, retries, Time Travel, official CI action, and report merging. Deductions reflect the small and concentrated community, upstream-fork lag, CDP-only mocks/accessibility, uneven non-Chrome isolation, stale dependency majors/docs examples, missing security governance, and project-specific lifecycle/download work. This is desk research, not an empirical benchmark.
evidence_and_decision.recommendation: Viable alternative. Testplane is current, feature-rich, and particularly strong where large screenshot suites, retries, sharding, and post-failure visual diagnosis dominate. It can test the Open Asset Allocator's HTMX/Navigo/Gin application without changing Parcel. It is not the recommended default because current adoption and independent support are much smaller than leading candidates, core behavior depends on a separately maintained WebdriverIO fork, and several project gates remain untested. Retain it for a focused spike if integrated open-source visual regression is valued more highly than ecosystem breadth.
evidence_and_decision.empirical_project_spike_result: [uncertain] Not performed. There is no empirical result in this repository for Node 24 plus TypeScript 6, HTMX node replacement and locator reacquisition, Navigo direct/deep/back routes, blur and native validation, Chart.js semantic and stabilized visual assertions, true browser downloads, REST fixture seeding, server-side Yahoo Finance replacement, PostgreSQL reset under retries/workers, or forced-failure screenshots, Time Travel, browser console, backend logs, and cleanup. These remain required before selection.
